draft_ledger.reference_answer:
Across the reported studies, pressure-driven nanofiltration (NF) and reverse osmosis (RO) membranes have achieved high, but clearly condition-specific, PFAS rejection in water and wastewater.

A review notes that available commercial NF and RO membranes treating water and wastewater "exhibited a good PFAS rejection in water and wastewater with efficiencies that could reach up to 99 %" (WF10_009_MMG001), indicating an approximate upper bound under favorable conditions rather than a universal value. In the same work, membranes operated in CCMF sequences with 97 % water recovery displayed overall PFAA rejection values of "> 98.3 %" for the assessed compounds (WF10_009_MMG001), showing very high removal for those specific PFAA and operating conditions.

Several NF studies provide more detailed, compound- and condition-specific benchmarks. A PMIA NF hollow-fiber membrane treating PFOS showed that raising pH from 3.2 to 9.5 increased PFOS elimination from 91.17 % to 97.49 %, and increasing Ca2+ from 0.1 mM to 2 mM further raised PFOS rejection from 97.10 % to 99.40 % (WF10_009_MMG002), illustrating that PFOS removal by this NF membrane can approach ~99 % under higher pH and ionic strength. Another study summarized in a table reports an NF lab test with a synthetic solution at 2 bar where PFOA rejection was 99 % (WF10_009_MMG004), and a functionalized MXene polyamide hollow-fiber NF membrane treating synthetic solution at 65 psi achieved 97.6 % PFOS rejection (WF10_009_MMG004). Commercial N90 and N270 flat-sheet NF membranes treating synthetic PFHxA solution at 4.8 bar achieved PFHxA rejection in the 89–99 % range (WF10_009_MMG004). In a coupled NF–electro-oxidation system, the NF step alone rejected 99.4 % PFHxA at an operating pressure of 20 bar (WF10_009_MMG003). Together, these NF results indicate that, under specific lab conditions with synthetic PFAS solutions at low to moderate pressures (2–20 bar or 65 psi), PFAS rejections on the order of roughly 90–99.4 % have been reported for PFOA, PFOS, and PFHxA.

RO studies likewise report very high, condition-dependent PFAS rejection. A lab-scale RO study using XLE, BW30, and SW30 polyamide flat-sheet membranes treating synthetic PFHxA solution operated at pressures from 6.9 to 55.2 bar with fluxes of approximately 15–90 LMH achieved PFHxA rejection greater than 98 % (WF10_009_MMG004). This provides a specific high-pressure RO example: under these lab conditions (synthetic PFHxA, 6.9–55.2 bar, ~15–90 LMH), PFHxA removal exceeded 98 %, demonstrating strong rejection but only for that particular configuration. Another lab RO study using ESPA3, LFC3, BW30, and SG polyamide flat-sheet membranes treating synthetic PFOS solution at 1380 kPa (with fluxes of 33–42 LMH) reported 99 % PFOS rejection (WF10_009_MMG004). At full scale, an RO system treating surface water achieved greater than 99 % rejection of PFOA and PFOS (WF10_009_MMG004). These RO results show that, in both lab and full-scale configurations, RO can reach around 99 % rejection for specific PFAS (PFHxA, PFOS, PFOA) under the documented pressures, fluxes, matrices, and membrane types.

Overall, the evidence indicates that pressure-driven NF and RO membranes have achieved PFAS rejections ranging from roughly the low 90% range up to about 99–99.4% for specific PFAS (including PFOA, PFOS, PFHxA, and PFAA mixtures) in synthetic solutions, water, and wastewater, at pressures from a few bar up to about 55.2 bar (or 1380 kPa) and with other operating variables such as pH, ionic strength, and recovery playing important roles. These values are explicitly tied to the particular compounds, membranes, matrices, and conditions reported and should not be generalized as universal performance for all PFAS or operating regimes.

Across the supplied studies, several examples show that background water chemistry and matrix components can change PFAS removal performance, but the effects are clearly described as PFAS‑specific, technology‑specific, and often modest, with explicit limitations on generalization.

For dissolved organic matter (DOM) and natural organic matrices, Shaikh et al. prepared a realistic background water matrix by matching the aqueous concentrations of background anions, cations, organic matter, and clay to a Ganga River water matrix to study their combined effect on PFOA adsorption by CTAB‑impregnated activated carbon adsorbents. In this realistic matrix, the adsorbent’s PFAS removal efficiency decreased from 98% to 88%. The authors state that humic acid and bentonite interact with the activated carbon and that “the 10% decrease in PFOA removal efficiency of the adsorbent can be attributed to silicate species, humic acid, and bentonite,” meaning these natural and mineral components act as competing species for adsorption sites. At the same time, they conclude that “the synthesized adsorbents exhibited good PFOA removal performance under realistic scenarios and can remove PFOA in the presence of higher background concentrations of typical water matrix species,” underscoring that while the realistic matrix reduces performance somewhat, PFOA removal remains high and the observed decrease should not be interpreted as a universal failure under natural-water conditions.

Other work links DOM in natural waters to reduced removal in membrane and adsorption systems but again underlines the context dependence. In a pilot‑scale nanofiltration (NF) study summarized by Taher et al., elimination of PFAAs using NF and RO membranes with spiked AFFF water was >98% and 99%, respectively. However, “changing the contaminated water source from spiked water to groundwater affected the removal efficiency of NF membrane and the rejection of the same PFAAs were removed by NF to a lower extent down to 92% due to the presence of other components in the groundwater, such as dissolved organic matters and Ca2+ that effect the interaction between functional groups of the PFAAs and membrane.” Here, natural groundwater constituents including dissolved organic matter and Ca2+ reduce NF rejection relative to a simpler spiked matrix, but the reported removal remains high, and the mechanism is described specifically for this NF system and set of PFAAs.

In an adsorption context, Ramos et al. evaluated biochars for PFAS removal from reclaimed water. They report that “for biochars generated in house, the removal performance decreased in treated municipal wastewater compared to DI water.” They interpret this as “consistent with previous observations that the ions prevalent in treated wastewater, as well as DOC, can decrease the PFAS adsorption capacity and performance of carbonaceous adsorbents due to pore‑blockage effects.” This explicitly links dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and co‑occurring ions in a realistic wastewater effluent to lower PFAS adsorption capacity. However, the effect is not uniform across PFAS: “the decrease in RE was almost non‑existent in the case of PFOS, which is likely due to the strong hydrophobic interactions that occur between the biochar surface and this compound.” Furthermore, they note that “adequate selection of the physicochemical properties of a biochar (e.g., Rogue biochar) can also mitigate the effects of competition between PFAS in mixed systems as well as the competition effects existing in more complex water chemistries.” These observations indicate that while DOC and ions can reduce PFAS uptake via pore blockage, the magnitude of the effect depends on PFAS structure (e.g., PFOS vs others) and sorbent properties and should not be extrapolated indiscriminately.

There are also cases where natural organic matter slightly improves apparent removal under specific conditions. In a nanofiltration study of PFOS using an NF270 membrane, Franke et al. reported removal efficiencies “between 94 and 97% for both deionized water and deionized water fortified with a humic acid concentration of 20 mg L−1” and noted that “they saw a slight increase in the removal efficiency for the humic acid containing PFOS solution as compared to the pure deionized water solution.” However, they caution that “comparisons to other studies should be made with care as many experimental parameters as well as water quality are often substantially different between studies.” Thus, the small beneficial effect of humic acid on PFOS removal is explicitly framed as context‑specific to their NF270 system and feedwater, not as a general rule for DOM in all PFAS treatments.

Regarding background cations and overall ionic composition, several studies highlight that ions can either hinder or enhance PFAS removal, depending on the treatment process and PFAS examined. The nanofiltration example summarized by Taher et al. explicitly attributes the reduction in PFAA rejection in groundwater (down to 92%) to “other components in the groundwater, such as dissolved organic matters and Ca2+ that effect the interaction between functional groups of the PFAAs and membrane.” This identifies Ca2+ as a key cationic component in natural groundwater that alters the interaction between PFAAs and the NF membrane, reducing removal compared to simpler spiked water.

In the biochar work described above, Ramos et al. connect decreased removal in treated municipal wastewater not only to DOC but also to “the ions prevalent in treated wastewater,” which “can decrease the PFAS adsorption capacity and performance of carbonaceous adsorbents due to pore‑blockage effects.” Here, the ionic strength and specific ions in the effluent are treated as contributors to competition and pore blocking in carbonaceous materials, but again the authors stress that the performance drop is PFAS‑dependent and can be mitigated by choosing a biochar with suitable physicochemical properties.

By contrast, Zhang et al. examined plasma‑based PFAS treatment in three real water matrices (tap water, wastewater effluent, and surface water), all spiked with the same PFAS mixture. They found that “the impact of water matrices on the removal of PFOA, PFOS, and HFPO‑TA is almost negligible (p > 0.05),” meaning that variations in background ions and other constituents among these waters did not significantly change removal for those three PFAS. However, “the removal efficiencies of PFHxA, PFHxS, and HFPO‑DA were found to be enhanced in different water matrices (p < 0.05).” The authors attribute these enhancements to the ionic composition: “the presence of salt in the actual water matrix exerts a favorable influence on the interfacial adsorption of PFAS, as it reduces the electrostatic repulsion between the ionic headgroups and increases the activity of the hydrophobic tail, thereby promoting the closer arrangement of PFAS molecules at the interface,” and “the increased conductivity of the actual water matrix results in a stronger electric discharge, further promoting the decomposition of PFAS.” These mechanistic interpretations are specific to their plasma reactor and PFAS set and, together with the negligible matrix effect for PFOA, PFOS, and HFPO‑TA, show that salts and conductivity can enhance removal of some PFAS but not others under the same treatment.

Another plasma‑based study by Eeso et al. compared PFOA and PFOS degradation in three landfill leachates, deionized water, and several groundwaters. They report that the average removal percentages of PFOA in leachates, deionized water, and groundwaters were 77, 72, and 52%, respectively, and those of PFOS were 64, 84, and 72%, respectively. Despite these differences, they state that “the water matrix did not have a big impact on the degradation of the two representative PFAS” and that “the small variations might be caused by factors such as the different concentrations of PFAS and PFAS precursors in the water matrix.” This explicitly frames observed differences as relatively minor matrix effects for PFOA and PFOS in their system and cautions against overinterpreting matrix‑induced changes without considering concentration and precursor differences.

For competing species beyond bulk DOM and salts, the Shaikh et al. adsorption study provides a clear example. Their selectivity study showed that “both humic acid and bentonite interact with the AC” and that “similar behaviour was observed for the realistic water background matrix as the humic acid and bentonite were adsorbed by the adsorbent.” They conclude that “the 10% decrease in PFOA removal efficiency of the adsorbent can be attributed to silicate species, humic acid, and bentonite,” indicating that these co‑present inorganic and organic particulates compete with PFOA for adsorption capacity. However, they also emphasize that even with these competing species, the adsorbents still offer “good PFOA removal performance under realistic scenarios,” highlighting that competition reduces but does not eliminate removal.

Ramos et al. similarly identify ions and DOC as competing species that decrease PFAS adsorption capacity and performance of carbonaceous adsorbents via pore blockage in treated municipal wastewater. Yet they observe that “the decrease in RE was almost non‑existent in the case of PFOS,” and that using a biochar with high surface area and favorable elemental ratios (Rogue biochar) “can also mitigate the effects of competition between PFAS in mixed systems as well as the competition effects existing in more complex water chemistries.” These results underline that competition effects from background solutes are not uniform across PFAS and can be partly managed by sorbent design.

Ammonia is mentioned only in the context of regeneration and not as a competing species affecting removal performance. Shaikh et al. report that to desorb PFOA by weakening electrostatic interactions from PFOA‑loaded adsorbents, they tested NaCl, NaOH, NH4Cl, KCl, and NH4OH solutions (5% w/v), and that NH4Cl and NH4OH achieved certain regeneration capacities. This speaks to the role of ammonium salts and bases in desorption during regeneration, not to their impact on PFAS removal from water. The provided evidence does not describe ammonia as altering PFAS removal efficiencies in the primary treatment step, so any inference of ammonia‑induced removal changes would go beyond the available data.

Finally, some studies explicitly limit how far their findings on background chemistry can be generalized. In addition to Eeso et al.’s statement that the water matrix did not have a big impact on PFOA and PFOS degradation and Zhang et al.’s finding that matrix effects on PFOA, PFOS, and HFPO‑TA removal were almost negligible, Franke et al. state that “comparisons to other studies should be made with care as many experimental parameters as well as water quality are often substantially different between studies.” Collectively, these caveats show that while background DOM, cations, ions, and co‑contaminants can reduce or sometimes enhance PFAS removal under specific conditions, the magnitude and direction of these effects are strongly dependent on PFAS identity, treatment technology, and detailed water chemistry, and should not be assumed to apply universally.

approved_source_evidence.full_chunk_text: 6    Conclusions and outlook 6.1    Conclusions This  review  provides  a  comprehensive  summary  of  the current  state  of  knowledge  on  the  PFAS  treatment  using electrochemical  processes,  including  electro-oxidation, electro-adsorption,  electro-coagulation,  and  coupled technologies. To better compare different electrochemical PFAS  removal  technologies,  the  removal  mechanism, energy  consumption,  and  key  operating  parameters  of these methods are summarized in Table S2. Based on the discussions  and  analysis  of  the  published  literature, several conclusions could be drawn, including: 1)  Electro-oxidation  system  usually  requires  a  high applied potential of > 3.0 V (vs. SHE) to induce electron transfer  from  PFAS  to  the  anode,  which  is  the  main reaction  pathway  for  its  degradation. Therefore, electrodes  must  be  anodically  stable. Nevertheless,  very few  low-cost  anodic  materials  can  maintain  high electrical  activity  over  a  long  period. It  remains  a challenge to find the electrode material not suffering from dissolution and disintegration at high potential, especially if it is made of toxic metals or nanomaterials (e.g., PbO2 and CNT). 2)  The  three  electrochemical  technologies  are  suitable for  different  application  scenarios  due  to  their  unique characteristics. For  example,  many  water  environments (e.g.,  groundwater)  containing  PFAS  have  low conductivity,  and  the  addition  of  supporting  electrolytes can cause secondary pollution.

draft_ledger.reference_answer:
In electro-adsorption-based PFAS treatment, the applied potential has a clear influence on adsorption behavior.

For adsorption behavior (Task T01), the review on electrochemical PFAS decontamination states that, under electro-adsorption conditions, ". . . the PFAS adsorption performance of an electrode increases with the increase of the applied voltage," and that this is associated with an improvement in the "adsorption capacity of the electrode" due to changes in the electrical double layer at the electrode–solution interface.[WF10_011_MMG003] This establishes that higher applied voltage generally enhances PFAS electro-adsorption performance and increases adsorption capacity, within the electro-adsorption operating window.

A specific example further illustrates the impact of applied potential on adsorption rate and capacity. For PFOA, the review reports that, compared with suspended MWCNT powder, an MWCNT electrode operated at an applied bias (0.6 V) shows a much higher initial adsorption rate and adsorption capacity.[WF10_011_MMG005] The paired values for the suspended powder and for the biased electrode demonstrate that imposing an electrochemical potential on the electrode can greatly enhance both the rate and capacity of PFOA adsorption compared with a non-electrified sorbent.

Other parts of the supplied evidence discuss how high applied potentials in electro-oxidation drive electron-transfer-based degradation,[WF10_011_MMG001, WF10_011_MMG002] or how applied voltage in electrocoagulation leads to PFAS removal via floc formation with colloidal particles,[WF10_011_MMG006] and how higher voltage can improve overall PFAS removal but is limited by water hydrolysis and energy efficiency.[WF10_011_MMG004] These statements concern degradation, bulk removal, or coagulation and are separate from the adsorption-rate and adsorption-capacity effects of applied potential described for electro-adsorption systems.
